29.title: The sun for breakfast
29.hook: baby Hanuman leaps for the sun, thinking it a mango; Indra's thunderbolt
29.howItsDone: Hanuman is one of the most widely worshipped figures in Hinduism; many Hindus visit his temples on Tuesdays or Saturdays, and his childhood stories are told to children as the start of his life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prasad, and a week with Ganesha. Your line was the offering comes back. Did something come back to you? This week belongs to another beloved god, and he starts out hungry. Day twenty-nine.

A baby wakes up hungry. His mother has gone to gather fruit. He looks around, and there, low on the horizon, is the rising sun: round, glowing, orange-red. It looks exactly like a ripe mango. So he jumps for it. Not a hop. This baby is the son of the wind, and he leaps straight up into the sky, higher and higher, reaching for breakfast. The gods watch in alarm. A child is flying at the sun with his mouth open. And Indra, king of the gods, lord of storms, does what a nervous king does. He throws his thunderbolt. It hits the baby on the jaw, and he falls, all the way down, to the earth.
screen: `A HUNGRY BABY.` → `THE SUN LOOKS LIKE A MANGO.` → `HE LEAPS.` → `INDRA'S THUNDERBOLT.`

segments.voice: The baby is Hanuman, and this is where his name comes from. Hanu means jaw in Sanskrit. Hanuman: the one with the jaw, the one who was struck. His name is the mark of the moment he reached too far. The story is told in the Ramayana, the great epic credited to the poet Valmiki, and in more than one place: an old bear, Jambavan, tells it to Hanuman himself later in the poem, and a later book tells it again. Some tellings say he thought the sun was a fruit; many families say a mango. Now listen to what happens next, because you've heard this shape before. Hanuman's father is Vayu, the wind. When his son falls, Vayu stops. He takes his child into a cave and simply stops blowing. And the whole world begins to suffocate. No breath anywhere. Just like Parvati's grief on day twenty-three, a parent's grief brings everything to a halt. So the gods come, all of them, and they heal the child, and each one gives him a gift: strength, speed, protection from weapons, a long life. Even Indra gives a gift. The baby who was knocked out of the sky goes home with more power than anyone. Look at the shape of it. The reach was too big. Of course it was. You can't eat the sun. But the tradition doesn't mock him for it. It names him after it. The wanting that sent him too high is the same wanting that, later, lets him leap an ocean. Reach anyway. You might fall. You might come home with gifts.
screen: `HANU — THE JAW.` · `TOLD IN THE RAMAYANA.` · `THE WIND STOPS.` · `EVERY GOD GIVES HIM A GIFT.` · then, large: `REACH ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with an appetite for too much. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you want that seems far too big. A dream you'd be embarrassed to say out loud. Don't shrink it. Don't argue with it. Just let it glow there, like the sun on the horizon, and notice how the wanting feels in your body. Then breathe slowly, like the wind that came back. The bell holds the time.
Hanuman, the one with the jaw, named for the moment Indra's thunderbolt struck him as he leapt for the sun. Healed after, with gifts from every god.
Your line: reach anyway. Today, take one small step toward the thing that seems too big. Just one. Day twenty-nine.

30.title: The forgotten strength
30.hook: cursed to forget his powers until reminded
30.howItsDone: Many Hindus recite the Hanuman Chalisa, a hymn traditionally credited to the poet Tulsidas, for courage in hard times; it retells Hanuman's deeds, including the crossing of the ocean.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sun for breakfast: Hanuman, a baby who leapt for the sun and came home with gifts from every god. Your line was reach anyway. Today, those gifts go missing. Day thirty.

So now you have a child with the strength of the wind, gifts from every god, and no sense of limits at all. Trouble follows. Young Hanuman runs wild through the forest hermitages where the sages live. He knocks over their water pots and ritual vessels. He tears their bark clothes. Not cruel, just a kid who doesn't know his own size. And the sages, patient people, reach the end of their patience. They don't take his strength away. They do something stranger. They put a curse on him: he will forget it. He'll have all that power, and not remember he has it, until someone reminds him.
screen: `A CHILD WITH NO LIMITS.` → `THE SAGES' PATIENCE ENDS.` → `HE WILL FORGET.` → `UNTIL SOMEONE REMINDS HIM.`

segments.voice: Years pass. Hanuman grows up gentle, wise, loyal, and he has no idea what he can do. Now jump ahead in the Ramayana. A band of monkeys and bears are standing on the southern shore, looking at the ocean. On the far side, somewhere, is the island of Lanka. Someone has to cross it. The text says a hundred yojanas, an enormous distance. One by one, the heroes say how far they could jump. Ten. Twenty. Fifty. Jambavan says ninety, now that he's old. The prince Angada says he could make the hundred, but isn't sure he could make it back. Nobody can do it. And Hanuman sits apart, quiet. He doesn't even volunteer. Then the old bear, Jambavan, walks over to him. And he tells Hanuman his own story. You are the son of the wind. As a baby you leapt for the sun. Every god gave you a gift. Why are you sitting here silent? And as Jambavan speaks, Hanuman remembers. The text says he begins to grow, swelling in size and strength, until the others cheer. Notice what the curse actually did. The strength was never gone. It was forgotten. That's a very different problem: forgetting what you've already survived, already done, already are. And notice how the curse is lifted. Not by a god. By a friend who remembers you better than you remember yourself. Sometimes that is what one person can do for another: tell them their own story back.
screen: `THE OCEAN NOBODY CAN CROSS.` · `HANUMAN SITS APART, QUIET.` · `JAMBAVAN TELLS HIM HIS STORY.` · `FORGOTTEN, NOT GONE.` · then, large: `YOU'RE STRONGER THAN YOU REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a strength you forget you have. Sit and breathe. Be your own Jambavan for two minutes. Remember a hard thing you got through. A time you were braver than you expected. Something you're good at that you stopped counting. Say it to yourself plainly, the way the old bear did: you did this. You are this. Then just sit with it, and let it grow a little. The bell holds the time.
Jambavan, the old bear who reminds Hanuman of his own forgotten strength, at the edge of the ocean where no one else could jump.
Your line: you're stronger than you remember. Today, be someone's Jambavan: remind one person of a strength they've forgotten. Day thirty.

31.title: Meeting Rama
31.hook: the disguised monkey meets the exiled prince
31.howItsDone: Hanuman is honored as the model devotee of Rama; in temples his image often kneels or stands before Rama, Sita and Lakshmana, and devotees chant Rama's name in his honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the forgotten strength, and an old bear who reminded Hanuman who he was. Your line was you're stronger than you remember. Whose Jambavan were you? Today, a meeting in disguise. Day thirty-one.

A mountain in the forest, and on it, a monkey king in hiding. Sugriva has been driven out of his kingdom by his own brother, and he's scared of everyone. One day he sees two men walking up the valley. Tall, dressed like hermits in bark, but carrying bows. Warriors in disguise, he thinks. Assassins, sent by his brother. So he sends his most trusted adviser to find out. Hanuman. And Hanuman goes in disguise too. He takes the form of a wandering holy man, walks down the mountain, bows to the two strangers, and starts asking polite, careful questions. Who are you? Why are you here? Two people, both hiding who they are, trying to read each other.
screen: `A KING IN HIDING.` → `TWO ARMED HERMITS.` → `HANUMAN IN DISGUISE.`

segments.voice: The two men are Rama and his brother Lakshmana. Rama is a prince in exile, and his wife Sita has been taken. You'll hear the whole story from its beginning in a few days; for now, that's enough. What's worth noticing is what happens when Hanuman speaks. In Valmiki's Ramayana, Rama turns to his brother and says, more or less: listen to him. Nobody talks like this without having studied deeply. Not one word out of place. Not too long, not too rushed. Every sentence clear and kind. Someone who speaks like this could win over an enemy with a raised sword. Rama recognizes Hanuman by how he talks, before he knows who he is. And Hanuman recognizes Rama. He drops the disguise, shows his true form, and in the Ramayana he lifts both brothers onto his shoulders and carries them up the mountain to meet his king. Later tellings go further. In the Ramcharitmanas, the retelling by the poet Tulsidas, Hanuman falls at Rama's feet the moment he knows him. In devotional tradition, this is where Hanuman's heart shows: from this meeting on, his life is devotion to Rama. That's bhakti, your sixteenth word, with a face. Look at how the knowing happens. Not by clothes. Both of them were in disguise. Each knew the other by how he spoke, what he noticed, how he treated a stranger. You know your people. And in this story, when Hanuman finds his, he picks them up and carries them home.
screen: `TWO DISGUISES.` · `RECOGNIZED BY HOW HE SPEAKS.` · `HE CARRIES THEM UP THE MOUNTAIN.` · `A LIFE OF DEVOTION BEGINS.` · then, large: `YOU KNOW YOUR PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with instant recognition of a good person. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you knew was good almost the moment you met them. What was it? The way they spoke to a waiter. The question they asked. The way they listened. Picture that first moment. Let yourself be grateful that you noticed. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Meeting Rama. Hanuman in disguise meets the exiled prince, and each knows the other by how he speaks. His life of devotion begins.
Your line: you know your people. Today, tell one of them what you noticed the first time you met. Day thirty-one.

32.title: The leap
32.hook: the ocean to Lanka; Surasa's mouth; the mountain that offers rest
32.howItsDone: Some Hindus read or recite the Sundara Kanda, the Ramayana's book of Hanuman's journey, as a devotional practice, sometimes in full over a day or across several days, especially in difficult times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, meeting Rama: two disguises, and a monkey who knew his prince by how he spoke. Your line was you know your people. Now Hanuman remembers his strength, and the ocean is waiting. Day thirty-two.

Hanuman climbs a mountain on the shore, grows huge, and presses down so hard with his feet that the rocks crack and the trees shake loose their flowers. Then he jumps. The text makes a spectacle of it: blossoms from the trees pulled along behind him, his shadow racing over the waves like a ship. He's flying to Lanka, to find Sita. And halfway across, a mountain rises out of the sea. Its name is Mainaka. It speaks. It says: you're doing a great thing for a good cause. Rest on me. Eat some fruit. Catch your breath. It's a kind offer. It's a real mountain. And it's right there.
screen: `HE CRACKS THE MOUNTAIN.` → `HE JUMPS.` → `A MOUNTAIN RISES: REST ON ME.`

segments.voice: Hanuman thanks the mountain. He touches it with his hand, politely, so as not to be rude, and says: I've made a promise; I can't stop. And he flies on. That's the first test of the leap: a good thing that would slow you down. The second test comes straight after. The gods send Surasa, the mother of serpents, to see what he's made of. She rises out of the water with her mouth open and says: nobody passes me without going into my mouth. So Hanuman grows bigger. She opens her mouth wider. He grows bigger. Wider. It could go on forever. And then Hanuman does the clever thing. He shrinks, suddenly, to the size of a thumb, darts into her mouth and straight back out, and bows. I went in. Now let me go. Surasa laughs and blesses him. That's the second test: not everything is won by getting bigger. Sometimes you get small and quick. There's a third test after that, a shadow-grabbing creature, Simhika, and he defeats her too. All of this is in the fifth book of Valmiki's Ramayana, the Sundara Kanda, the beautiful book. It's Hanuman's book, and some Hindus recite it whole, as a devotion, in hard times. So the leap isn't one jump. It's a string of small choices in the air: say no to the comfortable rest, don't get into a size contest, keep going. The leap is the practice.
screen: `THANK THE MOUNTAIN. FLY ON.` · `SURASA'S MOUTH.` · `GET SMALL AND QUICK.` · `THE SUNDARA KANDA.` · then, large: `THE LEAP IS THE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one leap you've been putting off. Sit and breathe. Name one thing you keep meaning to start. A call. A class. A hard conversation. Picture the mountain that keeps offering rest: later, not today, you've earned a break. Thank it, kindly, the way Hanuman did. Then picture the very first moment of the leap, just the first step. Breathe into that. The bell holds the time.
The leap. Hanuman flies the ocean to Lanka, declines the resting mountain, and slips through Surasa's mouth by getting small.
Your line: the leap is the practice. Today, take the first step of the thing you've put off, and say no to one comfortable rest. Day thirty-two.

33.title: Finding Sita
33.hook: the garden; the ring; "I'm not leaving without you"
33.howItsDone: The scene of Hanuman giving Rama's ring to Sita in the ashoka grove is often painted and performed, and it's a high point when devotees recite the Sundara Kanda.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the leap: a mountain turned down, and a thumb-sized escape from Surasa's mouth. Your line was the leap is the practice. Did you take a first step? Today, Hanuman lands. Day thirty-three.

Lanka at night. A city of gold, full of music and feasting and guards. Hanuman shrinks to the size of a cat and searches. Palace after palace. Room after room. He sees the demon king Ravana's wives asleep, and for a moment he thinks one of them might be Sita, and then stops himself: no. Sita would never be sleeping peacefully here. He almost gives up. Then, at the edge of the city, he finds a garden, a grove of ashoka trees. And under one tree, guarded by fierce women, sits a woman in a single worn cloth, thin from grief, refusing everything she's offered. He climbs into the branches above her and waits.
screen: `A CITY OF GOLD, AT NIGHT.` → `NOT HER. NOT HERE.` → `A GARDEN OF ASHOKA TREES.` → `A WOMAN UNDER A TREE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman has a problem. If a giant monkey drops out of a tree in the enemy's city and says, hi, Rama sent me, she'll scream, and he'll be caught. So he does something gentle. Hidden in the leaves, he begins quietly telling Rama's story, the story she knows best, in a soft voice. Sita looks up. Then he comes down, bows, and gives her the one thing that proves who he is: Rama's ring. She holds it, the text says, with joy, as though she had found her husband again. And then Hanuman makes an offer. Climb on my back. I'll carry you across the ocean tonight. You'll be with Rama today. It's easy to remember this moment as Hanuman saying: I'm not leaving without you. But in Valmiki, the one who says no is Sita. She won't go. She gives two reasons. She won't willingly touch any man but her husband. And she wants Rama to come himself, and end this properly. Then she takes a jewel from her hair and gives it to Hanuman, and tells him a small private story only Rama would know, so Rama will believe him. Ring in, jewel out. Weigh what crossed the ocean. Hanuman carried something tiny: a ring. Proof that she wasn't forgotten. In a city full of people telling her to give up, that ring said someone is coming. Bring the ring. Whoever is waiting for you needs proof you remember.
screen: `HE TELLS RAMA'S STORY, SOFTLY.` · `THE RING.` · `CLIMB ON MY BACK. SHE SAYS NO.` · `RING IN, JEWEL OUT.` · then, large: `BRING THE RING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a promise you keep quietly. Sit and breathe. Think of someone who is waiting on you. Maybe they don't even say so. A parent who waits for a call. A friend going through something. A child. What's the ring you could bring them: small, real proof that you haven't forgotten? Hold that person in mind for the whole sit. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Finding Sita. Hanuman finds her in the ashoka grove, gives her Rama's ring, and carries back her hair jewel as proof.
Your line: bring the ring. Today, send one small proof to someone who is waiting: a message, a call, a visit. Day thirty-three.

34.title: The burning tail
34.hook: caught, set on fire, burns Lanka with it
34.howItsDone: The burning of Lanka is a favorite scene in Ramlila performances across North India, and devotees recite it as part of the Sundara Kanda.

segments.voice: Yesterday, finding Sita: a ring in, a jewel out. Your line was bring the ring. Who got your proof? Today, Hanuman could just go home. He doesn't. Day thirty-four.

The job is done. He's found Sita. He has her jewel. He could slip away tonight and nobody in Lanka would know he'd been there. But Hanuman wants to see the enemy up close. So he does something loud. He tears up the royal garden, tree by tree, until the guards come. He fights off one wave of warriors after another. Finally Ravana's son, Indrajit, binds him with a divine weapon, and Hanuman, who could break free, lets himself be tied up and dragged into the court of the ten-headed king. He wanted to be caught. It was the only way in the front door.
screen: `THE JOB IS DONE.` → `HE TEARS UP THE GARDEN.` → `HE LETS THEM CATCH HIM.`

segments.voice: Standing before Ravana, Hanuman speaks plainly. Give Sita back. Make peace with Rama. It's the wise thing. Ravana is furious and orders him killed. But his younger brother, Vibhishana, objects: you don't kill a messenger. That's not how kings behave. Remember Vibhishana; he matters later. So Ravana chooses a humiliation instead. A monkey's pride is his tail, he says. Burn it. The guards wrap Hanuman's tail in rags, soak it in oil, set it alight, and parade him through the streets to laughter. And then Hanuman shrinks, slips his ropes, grows huge again, and leaps up onto the rooftops. With his tail blazing, he jumps from palace to palace, and Lanka, the golden city, goes up in flames. They handed him the fire. He used it. The text adds something tender. When Sita hears they've set his tail on fire, she prays to Agni, the god of fire, that it be cool for him. And Hanuman notices, mid-leap, that the fire isn't hurting him at all. Then a sudden panic: what if I've burned the garden where she is? He rushes back. She's safe. The fire went everywhere except to her. Notice who picked the weapon. Ravana chose the fire, to make a fool of him. Hanuman turned it into a message. Sometimes what's handed to you, the setback, the insult, the thing meant to shrink you, turns out to be exactly the tool you needed. Use what they hand you.
screen: `GIVE HER BACK.` · `DON'T KILL A MESSENGER.` · `THEY SET THE TAIL ALIGHT.` · `SITA PRAYS: BE COOL FOR HIM.` · then, large: `USE WHAT THEY HAND YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a setback used. Sit and breathe. Think of something that was handed to you as a setback. A rejection. A criticism. A plan that fell through. Then ask: what did it make possible? What did you learn, or build, or find, because of it? If you can't see anything yet, that's fine. Just hold it and ask: what could this fire light? The bell holds the time.
Lanka, Ravana's island city, set ablaze when Hanuman turns his burning tail from a humiliation into fire across its rooftops, Sita's prayer keeping it cool for him.
Your line: use what they hand you. Today, take one thing that went wrong and ask what it's good for. Day thirty-four.

35.title: The mountain of herbs
35.hook: can't remember which herb — brings the mountain
35.howItsDone: Many Hindus call on Hanuman as Sankat Mochan in times of trouble, visiting his temples, including the Sankat Mochan temple in Varanasi, and reciting the Hanuman Chalisa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lanka ablaze, the burning tail, and a humiliation turned into a message. Your line was use what they hand you. Today ends Hanuman's week, with a picture of him you may have seen: a monkey flying, holding a mountain. Day thirty-five.

Jump ahead, to the war for Lanka. Night on the battlefield. Rama's brother Lakshmana lies struck down by a terrible weapon, barely breathing. The healer in the camp says there's one hope: certain herbs that grow on a mountain in the Himalayas, far to the north. Bring them before sunrise, and he lives. It's a vast distance. Only one of them could cover it that fast. Hanuman goes. He crosses the land in the dark, finds the mountain, lands. And he stops. There are plants everywhere, glowing in the night. He doesn't know which ones are the herbs. And the sun will not wait.

So he picks up the whole mountain. Tears the peak off, balances it on one hand, and flies it back to the battlefield. The healer finds the herbs, and Lakshmana lives. That image, Hanuman in the sky with a mountain on his palm, turns up on calendars, temple walls and truck doors. Valmiki's Ramayana tells the herb-mountain journey in its war book, more than once, and later tellings, like the race against sunrise, add their own details. Today's word comes from this Hanuman. Sankat mochan. Sankat means trouble, a crisis, a tight spot. Mochan means release, setting free. The one who frees you from trouble. It's a name people call him by. In Varanasi there's a great temple by that name, and people who are frightened, sick, broke or grieving go and stand before him. Look at the choice he made. When he didn't know exactly what was needed, he didn't wait until he did. He brought everything. That's seva, your fifteenth word, at full size: service that doesn't do the minimum. Now look back at the week. A baby who reached for the sun. A strength forgotten, and a friend who remembered. A meeting where two disguises fell away. A leap made of small choices. A ring carried across an ocean. A fire turned into a message. And a whole mountain, because one leaf might have been the wrong one. Tomorrow, the Ramayana begins, from the very start.
